Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:36: And moreover, even one who has just begun to study and is proud of it, saying that he is a Torah scholar, his punishment is great, as we say in Tractate Bava Batra (98a): Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav, whoever is proud of a Torah scholar's cloak while not being a Torah scholar is not admitted into the enclosure of the Holy One, blessed be He - it is written here (Habakkuk 2:5), "a proud man, and he shall not abide [yinveh]," and it is written there (Exodus 15:13), "to Your holy abode [neveh]" - to this point. And it appears to me that this is measure for measure: just as he drove the Shechinah from his own house, so, when his soul ascends above, it shall be driven from the enclosure of the Holy One, blessed be He - for the Shechinah dwells only in a broken heart, and this is what they said in the Tikkunim (page 22b), that one must make a fine dwelling for it in his heart - meaning, that he be lowly and not angry - for once he is proud, the Shechinah flees from him, since he has given dominion to the maidservant in the place of her mistress - and therefore "he shall not abide" - just as there was no dwelling for the Holy One, blessed be He, in him, so there shall be no dwelling for his soul in the World to Come.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:37: And among the things that delay the redemption is haughtiness of spirit, as it is written in Sanhedrin (98a): Ze'iri said in the name of Rabbi Chanina, the son of David does not come until the haughty of spirit cease from Israel, as it is said (Zephaniah 3:11), "for then I will remove from your midst your proudly exultant ones, and you shall no longer be haughty on My holy mountain," and it is written, "and I will leave in your midst a poor and humble people, and they shall take refuge in the name of the LORD." And Rabbi Moshe of Coucy, peace be upon him, wrote in Klal 5, siman 64, concerning this matter - these are its words: and it does not mean an actually poor people, for it is written (Isaiah 60:9), "for the islands shall wait for Me, and the ships of Tarshish first, to bring your children from afar, their silver and gold with them" - but rather it means a humble people, and so Onkelos translated it, "a humble people" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:38: And after we have spoken of the disgrace of pride and its punishment, let us speak of the punishment of one who is angry - for anger comes only from pride of heart, for if his heart were broken and crushed, certainly he would not become angry and would not respond to his own disgrace, as we say at the end of our prayer, in "my God, guard my tongue from evil," "and to those who curse my soul, let my soul be silent, and let my soul be like dust to all" - and likewise in several matters, the punishments for anger are equal to the punishments for pride, such as that the angry person forgets his learning, as shall be explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:39: In Nedarim (22a) we say: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan, whoever becomes angry, all kinds of Gehinnom rule over him, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 11:10), "and remove anger from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh, for childhood and youth are vanity" - and there is no "evil" except Gehinnom, as it is said (Proverbs 16:4), "and even the wicked for the day of evil" - and moreover, intestinal ailments rule over him, as it is said (Deuteronomy 28:65), "and the LORD shall give you there a trembling heart, and failing of eyes, and languishing of soul" - what is a thing that fails the eyes and languishes the soul? Say, this is intestinal ailments. And the Rosh, of blessed memory, explained: "fails the eyes," that his illness is prolonged and he constantly looks forward to being healed - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:40: And we say further there: Rabbah bar Rav Huna said, every angry person - even the Shechinah is not considered important compared to him, as it is said (Psalms 10:4), "the wicked, in the haughtiness of his anger, will not seek Him," and so on. Rabbi Yirmiyah of Difti said, he forgets his learning and adds folly, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 7:9), "for anger rests in the bosom of fools," and it is written (Proverbs 13:16), "but a fool spreads out folly." Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said, it is known that his sins are more numerous than his merits, as it is said (ibid. 29:22), "an angry man stirs up strife, and a wrathful man abounds in transgression" - to this point. And so they said in Berachot (29b): Eliyahu said to Rabbi Yehudah, brother of Rav Sala the Pious, do not become enraged and you shall not sin - and the reason is, "a wrathful man abounds in transgression."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:41: And further we say in Pesachim (66b): Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said, every angry person - if he is a sage, his wisdom departs from him; if he is a prophet, his prophecy departs from him. If he is a sage, from where do we know this? From Moses, as it is written (Numbers 31:14), "and Moses was angry with the officers of the army," and so on, and it is written (ibid. 31:21), "and Elazar the priest said to the men of the army," and so on, "which the LORD commanded Moses" - implying that it had been hidden from Moses. And if he is a prophet, that his prophecy departs from him, from where do we know this? From Elisha, as it is written (II Kings 3:14), "were it not that I regard the presence of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would not look at you," and so on, "and now bring me a minstrel," and so on, "and the hand of the LORD came upon him," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:42: Rabbi Mani bar Patish said, every angry person - even if greatness is decreed for him from Heaven, he is brought down - from where do we know this? From Eliav, as it is said (I Samuel 17:28), "and Eliav's anger was kindled against David, and he said, why have you come down, and with whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your pride and the wickedness of your heart, for you came down to see the battle." And when Samuel went to anoint them, of all of them it is written, "the LORD has not chosen this one," but of Eliav it is written (I Samuel 16:7), "do not look at his appearance or the height of his stature, for I have rejected him" - implying that until now He had favored him - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:43: And further they said in Vayikra Rabbah (13:1): Rav Huna said, in three places Moses became angry and a halachah was hidden from him, and these are they: on the Sabbath, concerning an onen [mourner before burial], and concerning metal vessels. On the Sabbath, as it is written (Exodus 16:20), "and some men left over from it" - once he became angry, the laws of the Sabbath were hidden from him; what did he say to them? (ibid. 16:25), "eat it today, for today is a Sabbath to the LORD," and so on. And concerning metal vessels, "and Moses was angry with the officers of the army" (Numbers 31:14), and once he became angry, a halachah was hidden from him and he forgot to state the laws of metal vessels, until Elazar stated them. Concerning an onen, from where? (Leviticus 10:16), "and he was angry with Elazar and Itamar," and so on, and he forgot to tell them that an onen is forbidden to eat of the remaining sacred offerings - to this point. And they said in the Midrash HaShkem [an early midrash collection] concerning this matter: and if Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, of whom it is written (Numbers 12:7), "he is faithful in all My house," who conducted himself mercifully with Israel and gave his own life for them, saying (Exodus 32:32), "and if not, blot me out," and so on - father of the wise and the prophets - when he became angry for one hour, a halachah was hidden from him, how much more so ordinary people.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:44: And the reason for all these punishments, besides the reason already explained - that anger comes from the side of pride, and therefore what applies to one applies closely to the other - is further explained by Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Zohar (Parashat Tetzaveh, page 182a), from which the reason shall become clearer. He said there, on the verse (Isaiah 2:22), "cease from man, in whose nostrils is breath" - these are its words: and when the Holy One, blessed be He, created man, He made him in a supernal image, and breathed into him a holy spirit that includes three, as we have established, that he has nefesh, ru'ach, neshamah - and above all is neshamah, which is a supernal power to know and guard the commandments of the Holy One, blessed be He; and if that holy neshamah is brought into another service, this defiles it and it departs from the service of its Master, because these three powers are all one - nefesh, ru'ach, neshamah - joined together and becoming one, all in the pattern of the supernal secret, in accordance with what is said (Proverbs 13:20), "he who walks with the wise shall become wise." And if we see this person, in whom all these levels were found, before it is established with certainty who he is - by what is it known, when approaching this person, whether to withhold oneself from him? By his very anger one shall know him and recognize who he is - if he guards that holy neshamah at the time of his anger, so as not to uproot it from its place, so that a foreign god come to rest beneath it - behold, this is a person properly, this is a servant of his Master, this is a perfect man. But if that person does not guard it, and uproots this supernal holiness from its place so that the Other Side comes to rest in its place - certainly this is a person who rebels against his Master, and it is forbidden to draw near him or associate with him - and this is "he tears his own soul in his anger" - in his anger he tears and uproots his own soul because of his rage, and a foreign god comes to dwell within it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:45: And therefore it is written, "cease from man, in whose nostrils is breath [neshamah]" - for he tears that holy neshamah and defiles it because of his nose [anger] - "in whose nostrils" he exchanges it because of his nose. "For what is he accounted?" He is accounted as idolatry - and whoever associates with him and converses with him is as though he associates with idolatry itself. Why? Because idolatry itself dwells within him, and moreover, he has uprooted supernal holiness from its place and settled in its place idolatry, a foreign god - just as of a foreign god it is written (Leviticus 19:4), "do not turn to the idols," in this manner it is forbidden to gaze upon his face.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:46: And if you say, but there is anger for the sake of Torah scholarship? The anger of Torah scholars is good in every way, for we have learned that Torah is fire, and Torah boils him - as it is written (Jeremiah 23:29), "are not My words like fire, says the LORD" - the anger of Torah scholars is over matters of Torah, the anger of Torah scholars is to give honor to Torah, and it is all for the service of the Holy One, blessed be He. But if it is over other matters, this is not the service of the Holy One, blessed be He - for in all the sins a person commits, it is not idolatry itself, and it is forbidden to draw near him for this.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:47: And if you say, but this was only for a moment, and he transgressed and then returned - not so, for since he has uprooted the holiness of his soul from him and from its place, and that foreign god has strengthened itself within him and does not let him go - except if the person comes entirely and uproots it forever, and afterward strives to sanctify himself and draw holiness upon himself - only then, would that he be sanctified.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:48: Rabbi Yosei said to him, is he actually sanctified [immediately]? He said to him, come and see, at the time he uproots the holiness of his soul and the foreign god settles in its place, the person becomes impure and is called impure, and defiles whoever draws near him, and that holiness has fled from him - and since it has fled from him once, how much must a person do until it returns to its place? He said to him, if so, how impure are they who [nonetheless] become pure again? He said to him, this impurity differs from other impurity, which he cannot avoid causing, but this differs entirely from everything: it defiles the body within and without, and the soul, and defiles everything, whereas the rest of the impurity in the world affects only the body from without alone - and therefore, "cease from man, in whose nostrils is breath," for he exchanged the holiness of his Master because of his nose - and this is the impurity that defiles everything - "for what is he accounted?" - as idolatry, certainly he is accounted.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:49: Come and see, this anger is itself idolatry, the Other Side, as I have said, from which a person must guard himself and separate himself - and therefore it is written (Exodus 34:17), "you shall not make yourself a molten god" - "for yourself," to bring harm upon yourself - and it is written after it (ibid. 23:18), "you shall keep the feast of matzot" - this is the side of holiness that a person must guard, and not exchange it for the Other Side - and if he exchanges it, he becomes impure and defiles everyone who draws near him. "You shall keep the feast of matzot" - this is a place called "guard" [shamor], and therefore it is written, "you shall keep [tishmor] the feast of matzot" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:50: And when a person contemplates what Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in this teaching, that the angry person uproots all the holiness within him, which are nefesh, ru'ach, and neshamah, and because these three are one bond, Scripture calls them "his soul" [nafsho] - "he tears his own soul," and so on, and this is what it means, that the three powers are all one. And Rashbi, peace be upon him, informed us in this teaching of the greatness of the punishment, that we should not say the blemish is only in the nefesh alone but not in the others - for this is not so, but rather all the holiness within him departs, since once the husk rests in him, holiness flees, for he brings in and gives dominion to the maidservant in place of her mistress - since this is actually the sin of idolatry, and resembles the sin of idolatry that Israel committed when they brought an image into the Sanctuary, causing the Shechinah to flee from there, as is known.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:51: And therefore, since a foreign god, which is idolatry, comes to rest within him in a manner that defiles his body and soul, it is just that he forget his learning - for forgetting is the husk, as it is said (Genesis 40:23), "and the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:52: "And the Shechinah is not considered important compared to him" - as explained at the end of this teaching, concerning "you shall keep the feast of matzot - this is the side of holiness." And the matter is that "God has made this corresponding to that" (Ecclesiastes 7:14): just as the Shechinah is the inclusion of all the supernal attributes, and through her the arousal and dominion of the Cause of All Causes are shown, as explained in the Gate of Fear, chapter 1 - so too the foreign god, who is opposite her, includes within him all the powers of impurity, and he denies [divine] providence, as we explained in the Gate of Fear, chapter 8 - and therefore it said "all kinds of Gehinnom," for all of them are drawn from this husk, and all the other punishments are explained by this.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:53: Now, the Shechinah rests only upon a broken and crushed heart, and since he is angry, his heart is proud against him, and immediately the foreign god rests upon him, and he is the sum of all impurity - and therefore it said, it is forbidden to associate with him, because the worship of idolatry is called "sacrifices of the dead," and offerings to idolatry defile either by carrying or by [being in the same] tent, according to Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira, as they said in Tractate Chullin, first chapter (13a), concerning the slaughtering of a non-Jew - it is [like] a carcass, and defiles by carrying - they said there, it is taught, Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira says, from where do we know that an offering to idolatry defiles by [being in the same] tent? As it is said (Psalms 106:28), "and they attached themselves to Baal Peor and ate the sacrifices of the dead" - just as a corpse defiles by tent, so an offering to idolatry defiles by tent - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:54: And I heard from the mouth of Moreinu HaRav Yitzchak Ashkenazi, peace be upon him, that "he tears his own soul" means that he makes it a treifah [an animal with a fatal defect]. And one can be precise about this explanation from the language of the Zohar, which said, "that holy neshamah he tears and defiles because of his nose" - and its saying "defiles it," since it is a treifah, and a treifah is called dead, since a torn animal does not live twelve months (Chullin 57b), certainly it defiles - so too the angry person: since his holy soul was dwelling in his heart, once he brings in the husk, it is an adhesion that clings to it and defiles the soul. And so it says below, "and the soul, and everything, it defiles" - and it is not like an animal that is a treifah, which does not defile if it was slaughtered with a fit knife, but here he makes it a carcass [nevelah], slaughtering the soul with a blemished knife, which is Samael, SaM [poison] El [god], a foreign [zar] god.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:55: And one can also be precise about this explanation from the language of the Zohar, which said, "this is called 'he tears his own soul in his anger,' he tears and uproots his soul because of his rage" - and it said "uproots," meaning "uprooting the signs" [ikur hasimanim], which is one of the five things that invalidate ritual slaughter, making the animal a carcass and defiling by carrying - and just as "uprooting the signs" is uprooting the thing not in the customary order, but rather outside of nature, so is the angry person: for the essence of holiness naturally dwells in a person, since he was created for this, and this person, against its will, uproots it from its place. It follows that the word "tearing" has two explanations, and both are true.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:56: And it follows, along these lines, that the angry person, if he is a Kohen, makes himself impure with the impurity of a corpse - for all souls are from the side of Abraham, called "Kohen," as explained in Parashat Mishpatim (page 95a), that "the daughter of a Kohen" is the daughter of Abraham - and since he becomes angry, he kills his own soul, and the dead defile - it follows that a Kohen becomes defiled with the impurity of a corpse.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:57: Further, a warning to the angry person is found written in the verse (Psalms 81:10), "there shall be no foreign god within you," and so on - and it is explained in Tractate Shabbat (105b): Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chalafta ben Agra, who said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri: one who tears his garments in his rage, or breaks vessels in his rage, or scatters his money in his rage, shall be in your eyes like one who worships idolatry - for such is the craft of the evil inclination: today it tells him, do such-and-such, and tomorrow it tells him, go worship idolatry, and he goes and worships. And Rabbi Yochanan said, what is the verse? "There shall be no foreign god within you" - what is the "foreign god" that is within a person's own body? This is the evil inclination - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:58: And in the Zohar (Parashat Pekudei, page 263b), in the First Chamber of the Chambers of Impurity, they said - these are their words: and above these there is one appointed one named Sfasirita, and several treasurers of accounts, and this appointed one over them receives these evil words - and likewise he receives all those things a person throws with his hands when rage rests upon him, for then this appointed one, Sfasirita, takes that word a person casts in his rage, and ascends and says, this is the offering of so-and-so, brought to our side - because every side of tranquility is from the side of the right and from the side of faith, and every side of rage is from the Other Side, the evil side, the impure side - and therefore, whoever throws something from his hand in rage, all these take that thrown thing and raise it above and bring it near to that side, and they say, this is the offering of so-and-so - and a herald calls out through all those firmaments and says, woe to so-and-so, who has strayed after a foreign god and worshiped another god - and the herald calls out a second time and says (Hosea 6:12), "woe to them, for they have strayed from Me," and so on. Happy is the person who guards his ways and does not stray to the right or to the left, and does not fall into a deep pit from which he cannot rise - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:59: And through this teaching, Rashbi's teaching that we copied above, that "you shall keep the feast of matzot - this is the side of holiness," is explained more fully, and the language of guarding [shemirah] is mentioned in it, as explained above. And it is the Shechinah, called "matzah," which has no admixture of leaven, which are the husks, and is called "the feast of matzot" in her aspect on the right, which is Abraham, "Passover of the right arm" (Zohar, Parashat Ki Teitzei, page 282b) - and therefore Rashbi said, "every side of tranquility is from the side of the right and from the side of faith" - this is the secret of Israel's own craft, bound entirely to the Shechinah, as explained in the Gate of Fear, chapter 1 - and from the side of the right, as explained, whoever is not angry does not include himself on the side of judgment, while the angry person arouses the bile, which is the root of judgment, and therefore all kinds of Gehinnom rule over him, because he arouses judgment from its root, as it is written (Daniel 7:9-10), "a river of fire flowed and came forth from before Him" - and in the nose of Ze'ir [Anpin] there is a root for judgment, as it is written (Deuteronomy 32:22), "for a fire is kindled in My nose and burns to the depths of Sheol" - and the place where the river of fire is poured is in Gehinnom, "it shall whirl upon the head of the wicked," as explained in the Gate of Fear, chapter 13 - and therefore they said in the Tikkunim (page 85a) that the angry person is as though he kindled the fire of Gehinnom - these are its words, in Tikkun 48: happy is he who guards a fitting dwelling for the Sabbath, which is the heart, so that the sadness of the spleen and the anger of the bile, which is the fire of Gehinnom, not draw near there - of which it is said (Exodus 35:3), "you shall not kindle fire in any of your dwellings on the Sabbath day" - and this is certainly so, for whoever becomes angry is as though he kindled the fire of Gehinnom - to this point. And in the Ra'aya Meheimna (page 234, beginning of column 2) they explained this matter further; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:60: And when we are precise about the teaching that said, "and this appointed one over them receives these evil words, and likewise receives," and so on - these are two matters: "evil words" are the bad things said in anger, which a person casts suddenly from his mouth, for this appointed one is appointed only over anger, since over all matters of vulgarity another appointed one has already been mentioned above, and likewise over slander, mentioned below in the Third Chamber, and so on - and likewise he is appointed over things thrown from a person's hand, and this is the meaning of "and likewise receives" - for if these are similar matters, it would be fitting to say "and likewise" - so it appears to me. It follows that the blemish of anger is in the First Chamber of the husk, because he has blemished the mistress and enthroned the maidservant, who shall take her vengeance upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:61: And it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Tazria, page 43a) that once a person throws something from his hand in anger, from that hour he is handed over into the hand of the husk, and there is no blessing in the work of his hands - these are its words: come and see, it is forbidden for a person to throw the vessels of his house and consign them to the Other Side unnecessarily, or another similar matter, for several treasurers of accounts are ready for that thing to receive it, and from that time blessings do not rest upon him, since it is from the Other Side - and all the more so one who consigns his own supernal goodness to another, to the Other Side, for it belongs to whoever he consigned it to; and when a person's days draw near for him to leave this world, that supernal image given to him - that spirit that had attached to him every day comes, takes it, and it is repaired within it, and it goes its own way, and it never returns to the person again - then he shall know that he has been rejected from everything - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:62: And after we have spoken of the punishments of pride and anger, let us come to explain in a chapter of its own what things a person should consider in his mind so that he not come to anger, and so that he not respond to his own disgrace:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:1: The things a person should take to heart so that he not become angry are these. The first is what they, of blessed memory, explained (Pesachim 113b), and likewise in Chuppat Eliyahu (Gate of the Three): three the Holy One, blessed be He, loves: whoever is not angry, whoever does not become drunk, and whoever does not insist on his own rights - to this point. And the reason the Holy One, blessed be He, loves them is that these three are a chariot for Chesed, called love, as it is written (Jeremiah 31:3), "and I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have drawn you with kindness [chesed]."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:2: "Whoever is not angry" - it has already been explained above that the angry person arouses the power of the bile, which is the root of judgment, and it follows that he distances himself from Chesed. And likewise, one who becomes drunk is from the side of judgment, from the side of the harsh wine, from which love is not aroused - and whoever does not become drunk does not enjoy from the wine, which is judgment, but rather from what is close to arousing the love of Chesed, and therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, loves him. And likewise, whoever does not insist on his own rights is bound to Chesed, who does good both to the good and the wicked, since the Holy One, blessed be He, from the side of Chesed, does not repay a person according to his deeds, as it is written (Psalms 103:8-10), "the LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abundant in kindness; He will not always contend, nor keep His anger forever; He has not dealt with us according to our sins," and so on. And whoever insists on his own rights, deserving to be repaid measure for measure, is bound from the side of judgment, which is exacting, to give to each man according to his ways and the fruit of his deeds. And these three are the three lines in their order, from the side of prevailing Chesed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:3: And the merits that one who does not insist on his own rights has are these: first, that he lives long in this world; further, that his transgressions are forgiven, as we learn in Tractate Megillah (28a) - Rabbi Akiva asked Rabbi Nechunya the Great, through what have you lived long? He said to him, in my days I never accepted gifts, never insisted on my own rights, and was yielding with my money. This is like Rabbi Elazar, who, when they would send him gifts from the Nasi's house, would not accept them, and when they would invite him, would not go, saying to them, you do not wish that I live, for it is written (Proverbs 15:27), "and he who hates gifts shall live." Rabbi Zeira, when they would send to him from the Nasi's house, would not take, but when they would invite him, would go, saying, they honor themselves through me. "And never insisted on my own rights" - for Rava said, whoever does not insist on his own rights has all his transgressions forgiven, as it is said, "who bears iniquity and passes over transgression" - for whom does He bear iniquity? For whoever passes over transgression - to this point. And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained on this saying in Tractate Rosh Hashanah (17a): "one who does not insist on his own rights" - who does not exact measure for measure from those who trouble him, but rather sets aside his rights and moves on, like [the principle], "one does not [make a fuss and] pass over other mitzvot [to fulfill this one]," "one does not pass over foods [worrying over each]" - he sets them aside and moves on. "His transgressions are passed over for him" - the attribute of judgment does not scrutinize them, but rather sets them aside and moves on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:4: And further they said in Sanhedrin (92a) - these are their own words: and Rabbi Elazar said, always be among the humbled and sustained [i.e. accept humiliation and you shall endure] - meaning, be lowly and you shall live; and certainly whoever is lowly is humble and does not insist on his own rights.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:5: And further, a third merit is that he is saved from a strange death, as they said in the Zohar (Parashat Miketz, page 201b) concerning a certain man who had this merit and was saved from a strange death - these are its words: Rabbi Abba was sitting at the gate of Lod, and he saw a certain man coming to sit in a hollow hanging from the ground - he was weary from the road and sat and slept there. Meanwhile he saw a serpent coming toward him; a weasel came out and killed the serpent. When that man awoke, he saw that serpent before him, dead, and that man stood up, and that hollow fell into the depth beneath him, and he was saved. Rabbi Abba came to him and said, tell me what your deeds are, for the Holy One, blessed be He, performed for you these two miracles - they are not for nothing. That man said to him, all my days no wicked person has ever completed his day against me without my having made peace with him and forgiven him - and moreover, if I was unable to make peace with him, I would not go up to my bed until I had forgiven him and all who troubled me, and I would not worry, all day, about the evil that had happened to me; and it was not enough for me, but from that day onward I would strive to do good to them. Rabbi Abba wept and said, this man's deeds are greater than Joseph's - Joseph's were certainly his brothers, and it was fitting for him to have mercy on them, but what this one does is greater than Joseph, and it is fitting that the Holy One, blessed be He, perform for him miracle upon miracle - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:6: And I found written that this attribute, which was in this pious man, was also in [a certain] Rav, and it is counted among ten attributes he had, one of them being that whoever provoked him, he would go and appease him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:7: And so Rabbeinu Yonah, peace be upon him, wrote in Sefer HaYirah - and these are its words: be conciliatory to your brother and your fellow, and do not go to sleep at night with a quarrel between you and another person; rather, go and appease him until he is reconciled - and even if he sinned against you, seek reconciliation from him, and do not say, he sinned against me, so it is he who should appease me - subdue your inclination and go to him, so that your heart not become proud and you become an abomination before the Creator, as it is said (Proverbs 16:5), "every proud heart is an abomination to the LORD."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:8: Further, a fourth merit: that his decree is torn up and life is added to him - that if he became ill and was near death, and they examined his deeds and found this merit for him, he is saved from death to life - and so they said in Tractate Rosh Hashanah (17a) - these are their own words: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, became ill. Rav Pappa went to inquire about him and saw that his condition was hopeless. He said to them, prepare his provisions [for burial]. In the end he recovered. Rav Pappa was ashamed to see him. He [Rav Huna] said to him, what did you see? He said to him, so it was [I thought]. He said to them, the Holy One, blessed be He, said, since he does not insist on his own rights, do not insist strictly on My part against him, as it is said (Micah 7:18), "who bears iniquity and passes over transgression" - for whom does He bear iniquity? For whoever passes over transgression - "for the remnant of His heritage." Rabbi Acha bar Chanina said, [there is] honey, but also a thorn in it - "for the remnant of His heritage," and not for all His heritage - only for one who makes himself like the remnant [i.e., humble] - to this point. And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "prepare his provisions" - prepare for him provisions for the road, meaning, the provision of the dead is shrouds. "Recovered" - was healed. "So it was" - death had been decreed upon me. "Does not insist on his own rights" - does not stand firm on his own claims. "Do not insist strictly against him" - do not scrutinize him. "Honey, but a thorn in it" - meaning, there is a matter of comfort here, but there is a hard thing within it that does not apply equally to all - to this point. And in the Midrash Ruth (Zohar Chadash) they brought a similar story about Rabbi Karuspedai, who became ill and was near death, and departed to that world, and was, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:9: And in Chuppat Eliyahu they brought a story close in language, of the same matter, concerning the teaching we copied at the beginning of the chapter - three the Holy One, blessed be He, loves, and so on - these are its words: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, became ill, and lingered in that world for several nights and several days; when he returned, they said to him, Rabbi, through what were you released? He said to them, my children, happy is he who does not insist on his own rights - by the [divine] service, companies of ministering angels came and taught merit on my behalf, and it was not accepted from them, until an angel came and said, on behalf of whom are you teaching merit? Is it not on behalf of this one who never insisted on his own rights? Immediately they released me from death to life.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:10: Further, there, close to this, they brought a wondrous story about one who does not insist on his own rights - these are its words: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak had a mound of earth within his vineyard, and he brought workers there to dig the mound - they dug it that whole day. On the second day, as they were digging, a certain man leaped from within his house and sat upon the mound and began to sway and cry out - and what was he crying out? Perhaps the resurrection of the dead has arrived, perhaps the resurrection of the dead has arrived! The workers ran and informed Rav Nachman. He came and found him. He said to him, who are you? He said to him, I am dead - perhaps the time of the resurrection of the dead has arrived. He said to him, what is your business at this mound? He said to him, did I not tell you, I am dead? He said to him, but a dead man does not decay? He said to him, did they not bring you into the house of study and read to you the Book of Proverbs, and did not Solomon say (Proverbs 14:30), "and envy rots the bones"? In my days I never insisted on my own rights, and I never harbored envy of my fellow in my heart, and I never gossiped, neither in the study hall nor in the synagogue, and I gave my heart and my eyes only to words of Torah, to fulfill what is said (ibid. 1:33), "but whoever listens to me shall dwell securely." Rav Nachman said to him, I shall build you a domed structure. He said to him, do not do anything for me, and do not remove me from this place, for I was buried with permission - rather, return the dust that was removed from over me to its place. And Rav Nachman was frightened and grieved the entire day, saying, woe to me, perhaps I have offended that dead man. Immediately he saw in a dream that he was sitting in a sukkah of myrtle branches. He immediately gave praise and thanks before the Holy One, blessed be He, and read this verse (ibid. 8:34), "happy is the man who listens to me, watching daily at my doors" - praised be the name of the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, who withholds the reward of no creature - and if this one, who had in his hand only the reward of silence alone, and did not insist on his own rights, was repaid thus by the Holy One, blessed be He, how much more so shall the Holy One, blessed be He, repay double and doubled the reward of one who accustoms himself to the study of Torah, raises his children to the study of Torah, and walks in [divine] service and lowliness of spirit - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:11: Further, a sixth merit: that the prayer of one who does not insist on his own rights is heard, as is proven in Ta'anit (25b) - it says there, a story of Rabbi Eliezer, who went down before the ark and said twenty-four blessings [of supplication] and was not answered; Rabbi Akiva went down and said "Avinu Malkeinu" and was answered. A heavenly voice went out and said, it is not that this one is greater than that one, but that this one does not insist on his own rights, and that one does not [i.e., does] insist on his own rights - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:12: And further, a seventh merit: that the world endures through it, as explained in Tractate Chullin, end of chapter 6 (89a): Rabbi Ilai said, the world endures only through him who restrains his mouth at a time of quarrel, as it is said (Job 26:7), "He hangs the earth upon nothing [belimah]" [a play on "restraint," bal + peh]. Rabbi Abahu said, through him who makes himself as though he were nothing, as it is said (Deuteronomy 33:27), "and underneath are the everlasting arms" - to this point. And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "restrains" - stops up his mouth. "And underneath" - whoever is trodden underneath everyone else, he is the "arms of the world."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:13: Further, the eighth and ninth merits: that he shall merit Torah, and that Elijah shall be revealed to him - for Torah is explained only to whoever is not exacting, and Elijah is revealed only to whoever is not exacting, as explained in Tractate Kallah Rabbati, Chapter "Judge Your Own Words Favorably" (chapter 5) - these are its words: Abba Eliyahu, of blessed memory, said, Torah is explained only to whoever is not exacting; I too am revealed only to whoever is not exacting - happy is whoever encounters him, and whoever sits with him, for he is assured of a portion in the World to Come - to this point.
